item.title: How to Build AI Agents with the n8n Agent Builder: From Zero to a Working Agent
item.description:
Introduction

For years, building an AI agent in n8n meant assembling one inside a workflow canvas: a Chat Trigger, a memory node, an AI Agent node, a language model, and a pile of tools wired together by hand. That pattern still works, but n8n now offers a dedicated Agent Builder, a separate surface where the agent itself is the artifact. You describe the agent’s purpose in plain language, choose its model, attach tools, configure memory, connect channels such as Slack or Telegram, and publish it. This tutorial walks you through that full flow, from an empty builder to a working agent with workflows mounted as tools and human approval guarding the risky steps.

item.title: How to Use n8n Workflows as MCP Tools in Claude Code
item.description:
Introduction

Claude Code writes great code, but your n8n workflows already encode the automations that matter: the newsletter pipeline, the CRM sync, the deploy checks. n8n’s built-in, instance-level MCP server turns those workflows into tools Claude Code can search, inspect, and execute. This tutorial covers enabling the server, connecting Claude Code with OAuth or an API key, exposing your first workflow, and running it from the terminal, on n8n Cloud and self-hosted instances alike.

item.title: Meta WhatsApp Business MCP Server Setup: Let an AI Agent Onboard Your Business Number
item.description:
Introduction

Setting up WhatsApp Business messaging used to mean four open tabs: the Meta Developer Console, Business Manager, the API reference, and your code editor. On September 15, 2026, Meta shipped the WhatsApp Business Tools MCP server, which hands that entire sequence to an AI agent. This tutorial shows you how to connect the server to Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, or ChatGPT, authenticate with OAuth, and onboard a phone number, create templates, and configure webhooks by describing what you want in chat.

item.title: Make.com MCP Server Tutorial: Turn Your Scenarios into AI Tools
item.description:
Introduction

Your Make scenarios already automate the boring parts of your business. This tutorial shows you how to expose those scenarios as tools that an AI agent can call directly from Claude, ChatGPT, or Cursor. By the end, you will have connected the Make MCP server, published a scenario as a callable tool with a well-designed input schema, locked the agent down to exactly the scenarios it needs, and handled the timeout behavior that trips up most first-time setups. It is written for Make users who already build scenarios and now want agents to run them.

item.title: MCP Postgres Server Tutorial: Safe Read-Only Database Access for AI Agents (2026)
item.description:
Introduction

Letting an AI agent touch your database is the fastest way to make it useful and the fastest way to lose data. One hallucinated UPDATE without a WHERE clause is all it takes. This tutorial shows the setup that earns both: an AI assistant that can explore schemas, run analytical queries, and explain slow query plans against PostgreSQL, while two independent layers stop it from writing anything. You will install the actively maintained Postgres MCP Pro server, create a least-privilege read-only database role, and lock the server into restricted mode. It is written for developers who already know what an MCP server is; if you do not, start with our Model Context Protocol pillar guide first.

item.title: MCP Stateless Spec Migration Guide: Move Your Server to 2026-07-28 Without Downtime
item.description:
Introduction

If you run an MCP server built on the 2025-era Streamable HTTP transport, your request lifecycle starts with an initialize handshake and depends on a sticky Mcp-Session-Id header for everything that follows. On 28 July 2026 the Model Context Protocol shipped revision 2026-07-28, which deletes both of those concepts and makes every request self-describing. MCP co-creator David Soria Parra calls it “[MCP’s] most important [release] since remote MCP first launched.” This guide migrates your server to the new stateless wire: what to delete, what to implement (server/discover, per-request _meta, the new headers), how to keep 2025-era clients working during the transition, and how to regression-test the whole thing. It is written for developers who already operate an MCP server over Streamable HTTP. If you have never built one, start with our Model Context Protocol pillar guide first.

item.title: How to Build an MCP Server in Python (2026): Tools, Resources, and Claude Desktop Setup
item.description:
Introduction

Building an MCP server in Python is the fastest way to give an AI assistant access to your own data and actions: your notes, your database, your internal APIs. The official Python SDK does almost all the protocol work for you. You write small, type-hinted Python functions, and the SDK turns them into tools with JSON schemas, validates every call, and speaks the Model Context Protocol to any host. This tutorial walks through the current SDK (v2, which supports the 2026-07-28 MCP specification) from an empty folder to a working server connected to Claude Desktop, with testing and the five mistakes everyone makes.

item.title: Claude Code MCP Setup: Connect Any MCP Server in Minutes
item.description:
Introduction

Claude Code is Anthropic’s terminal-native coding agent, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is how you plug it into everything outside the terminal: issue trackers, databases, design tools, monitoring dashboards. This tutorial sets up MCP servers in Claude Code from scratch, picking the right scope, writing the exact CLI commands, and verifying the connection. Every command below was run against a real Claude Code 2.1.283 install on 2026-09-28, and the transcripts are the actual output.

item.title: How to Add an MCP Server to Cursor
item.description:
Introduction

Adding an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server to Cursor gives the AI agent access to tools outside your codebase, a filesystem reader, a database, a web fetcher, your GitHub issues. This guide walks you through the full process using a real example server, verified against the official Cursor docs, and ends with a test you can run in Agent chat to prove it works.

Quick answer

To add an MCP server to Cursor, create a .cursor/mcp.json file in your project (or ~/.cursor/mcp.json for all projects) with a top-level {"mcpServers": {...}} object describing each server, then restart Cursor and confirm the green status dot on Cursor Settings → MCP. The steps below show the exact JSON and how to verify the connection.

item.title: How to Connect an MCP Server to Claude Desktop (Step-by-Step)
item.description:
Introduction

Connecting an MCP server to Claude Desktop turns Claude from a chatbot that only talks about files into an assistant that can actually work with them, reading folders, editing documents, querying databases, or calling APIs through tools you install. This guide is for macOS and Windows users who already have Claude Desktop installed and want a server up and running in about ten minutes. You’ll add the official filesystem MCP server, the canonical first example from the Model Context Protocol documentation, verify that Claude can see its tools, and learn the fixes for the three connection problems that account for nearly every “my server doesn’t show up” report.

item.title: Windsurf MCP Setup: Connect MCP Servers to Windsurf
item.description:
Introduction

Windsurf’s Cascade agent becomes dramatically more useful once you connect MCP servers: instead of only seeing your local files, Cascade can fetch web pages, query databases, and call external APIs through tools that MCP servers provide. This tutorial walks you through the complete Windsurf MCP setup, finding the right config file, writing valid JSON, adding a real working server, and fixing the errors that trip up most first-time setups. It is written for developers who already use Windsurf (or the newer Devin Desktop builds) and are comfortable editing a JSON file and running a terminal command.
